newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government, opposition look set for tax talks.
newsitem.headline: German government, opposition look set for tax talks.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) looked set on Thursday to meet later this month to try to break deadlock over plans for a comprehensive tax reform.
The SPD greeted an offer by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to bring forward the start of his planned income tax reform by one year to 1998 as a step in the right direction.

But SPD leaders stood by their demand that the whole package -- which aims for a 30 billion mark ($18 billion) net tax cut and to simplify the tax system -- should be implemented in 1998 and not just parts of it, as Waigel indicated.

"Because of the strong dollar, exports are going okay, but mass purchasing power in Germany is so bad that demand is faltering," said Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, economics spokeswoman for the SPD parliamentary faction.
"That is why we need tax cuts for the broad masses of the employed in 1998 ... What (Waigel) said goes in the right direction, but only half way," she said in a radio interview.
The SPD also remains opposed to any increase in value-added tax to finance part of the planned tax cuts.

Waigel, under pressure to win SPD support for tax reform, offered on Wednesday to accelerate tax reform. He also needs to cut spending to plug a widening budget deficit due to record unemployment and a weak German economy.

Waigel proposed lowering the entry level income tax rate "in the direction of 20 percent" next year from 25.9 percent now, and to cut the top rate to below 50 percent. The fuller plan calls for cutting the top rate to 39 percent.

SPD faction chief Rudolf Scharping said he hoped to hold talks this month with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition parties to break the standstill in the tax debate. The SPD hoped to cut tax rates for corporations as well as individuals, he said.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats, responded to Scharping by saying he expected the coalition to offer to talk to the SPD about the tax reform this month.
Hintze said the aim would be to agree a tax relief programme which could start in 1998. "This is an important project for growth and employment and more jobs," he said on German television.

Gerhard Schroeder, the SPD prime minister of Lower Saxony, told the Handelsblatt newspaper in an interview to appear on Friday that he approved of the principle of cutting the top tax rate on commercial income to 35 percent.
But he was sceptical about whether the top tax rate on other forms of income should be reduced to 39 percent.
The SPD was not intent on leaving the top tax rate for non-commercial income at 53 percent. But the extent to which it could be cut would depend on cutbacks in other tax allowances.
On Wednesday, Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said the government wanted to present a draft tax bill in April and hoped SPD talks could begin "three or four weeks after Easter".
Matthaeus-Maier criticised Bohl, saying the SPD was prepared to talk immediately. Unnecessary delays to talks could bog down the whole process, she said.

She also took issue with Kohl's statement on Wednesday that workers should do without real wage increases to help create new jobs. "There haven't been any (real wage rises) for years, and that's why people need ... tax cuts," she said.

Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, accused the SPD of playing politics before elections in 1998 by appearing ready to compromise while blocking real progress.

"(SPD chairman Oskar) Lafontaine is pursuing a scorched-earth policy," he said in a radio interview. "He wants to let everything fail, so that in 1998 he can say, 'Look, it didn't work,' while he himself was the cause."
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
